article_title: Are all biases bad? Collaborative grounded theory in developmental evaluation of education policy
citation: Anderson, R., Guerreiro, M., & Smith, J. (2016). Are all biases bad? Collaborative grounded theory in developmental evaluation of education policy. Journal of Multidisciplinary Evaluation 12(27), 44-57.
title: Varied perspectives should be a critical component in the methodological and analytical choices of education research when the goal is deeper understanding of program or policy impact
description: This principle holds that education research should deliberately build varied perspectives into its methodological and analytical choices. The authors argue that "varied perspectives should be a critical component in the methodological and analytical choices of education research", especially "when the sought after outcome is deeper understanding of the impact, both positive and negative, of an education program or policy". It directs evaluators to treat interpretive diversity as a design feature rather than a threat to be controlled.
requirements: At least two researchers with distinct perspectives participating in analysis and theory generation
constraints: Argued for in the context of education policy and program evaluation seeking deeper understanding of impacts
target_learning_goals: deeper understanding of the positive and negative impacts of education programs and policies
examples: In the study, two researchers with distinct perspectives cogenerated themes and theory from interviews of education leaders in Kentucky and California.
key_sources: Anderson, R., Guerreiro, M., & Smith, J. (2016). Are all biases bad? Collaborative grounded theory in developmental evaluation of education policy. Journal of Multidisciplinary Evaluation 12(27), 44-57. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/are-all-biases-bad-collaborative-grounded-theory-in-developmental-evaluation-of-education-policy/

article_title: Using Technology to Support Postsecondary Student Learning
citation: Dabbagh, N., Bass, R., Bishop, M., Costelloe, S., Cummings, K., Freeman, B., Frye, M., Picciano, A. G., Porowski, A., Sparrow, J., & Wilson, S. J. (2019). Using technology to support postsecondary student learning: A practice guide for college and university administrators, advisors, and faculty. Washington, DC: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Use varied, personalized, and readily available digital resources to design and deliver instructional content
description: The guide recommends leveraging technology to vary, blend, or accelerate course formats and to package course content to minimize cost, maximize accessibility, and accommodate different learning preferences. It argues that formats requiring students "to be in a specific place, at a specific time, and for a fixed duration necessarily bound opportunities for interaction." Blended and flipped formats can preserve class time for hands-on activities, group assignments, and individualized instruction, and interactive modules can provide immediate feedback through adaptive learning features.
requirements: Align course delivery structures with course content and the students taking the course
Use design frameworks such as ADDIE to develop flexible delivery formats aligned with course goals
constraints: Rated moderate evidence based on 16 studies (eleven meeting WWC standards without reservations, five with reservations)
Planning online education requires attention to institutional context, available finances, and hardware and software
target_learners: postsecondary students, including those in developmental and accelerated course pathways
target_learning_goals: deeper engagement with course content and flexible access to learning materials
examples: The Open Learning Initiative (OLI) Statistics course in an accelerated blended format, and Time Compressed Animated Delivery (TCAD) of follicular dynamics in reproductive physiology

article_title: To Create Safe and Healthy Schools during a Pandemic, Prioritize Educator Wellbeing
citation: Browning, A., & Romer, N. (2020). To create safe and healthy schools during a pandemic, prioritize educator wellbeing. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Validated wellness measures for surveying educator wellbeing (Teacher Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire, Professional Quality of Life Scale)
description: The brief names validated instruments schools can use to regularly survey and assess the wellness needs of educators: the Teacher Subjective Wellbeing Questionnaire, the Professional Quality of Life Scale, and the California School Climate, Health, and Learning Surveys. Results are to be used to identify individual and collective needs brought to the attention of school leaders. Paradise Unified School District's staff screening with the Professional Quality of Life Scale found a large number suffered from secondary trauma, prompting new staff wellness supports.
requirements: Use a validated wellness measure or school climate survey rather than ad hoc questions
Use results to identify individual and collective needs for school leaders
target_learning_goals: assessing educator wellness needs
identifying staff secondary trauma and support needs
examples: Paradise Unified School District's fall 2019 universal screening of students and staff following a devastating fire used the Professional Quality of Life Scale for staff

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Valor Collegiate Academy Compass Model with badge system and Compass Circles
description: The Compass Model is Valor Collegiate Academy's whole-school SEL and mental health approach, consisting of five interdependent domains that help students develop an inner compass for a purposeful life. Students earn badges marking key disciplines, habits, and mindsets from 5th grade to graduation, and participate in weekly Compass Circles of 15 to 20 students facilitated by a mentor. Survey data showed "more than 80% of students report that Circles help them feel less alone," and approximately 80% of faculty reported the program changed how they think about emotions; 64 schools have adopted the model.
requirements: Weekly peer groups (Compass Circles) facilitated by a mentor
integration with the academic curriculum and student choice of pathways
constraints: The report describes Valor as intentionally diverse by income and race since opening in 2014, serving Grades 5-12 in Nashville, Tennessee
target_learning_goals: Positive identity development
self-awareness and social awareness
purpose, kindness, determination, and curiosity
examples: Valor has ranked in the top 5% of Tennessee schools in growth and achievement since 2014, with lower socio-economic students outperforming middle- and upper-income peers in the state

article_title: A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process
citation: Melinda Wallace and Sheila Arredondo. (2022). A Standardized, Equitable, and Transparent High-Quality Instructional Materials Review Process. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567789
title: State instructional materials review designed around statewide core values of equity, access, inclusivity, community, and transparency
description: The refined Nevada process organizes materials adoption around the SEA strategic plan's core values — "equity, access to quality, success, inclusivity, community, and transparency" — and defines high-quality curricula as standards-aligned and culturally engaging: accurate, content-rich, free from bias, and supportive of students' linguistic and cultural lenses. The design responds to prior review inequities, especially for rural districts, by standardizing rubrics, training, and public participation opportunities.
requirements: Review process design must define reviewer qualifications and trainings, process timing, public participation opportunities, and consistent reviewer expectations
constraints: What counts as high quality is defined against Nevada's own statutes, strategic plan, and NVACS; the report draws on approaches from eight other states and organizations such as RAND, Achieve, EdReports, and WestEd
target_learners: K-12 students, including students from different experiences and backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Improved learning outcomes through access to high-quality curriculum
examples: NDE and R15CC designed the process using district-leader interviews, other states' approaches, research from RAND and others, OER Commons study, and pilot reviews of primary core materials

article_title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: How AI Could Disrupt the Regeneration of Professional Expertise
citation: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602
title: The Validation Tether and the Internalized/Distributed Mastery distinction
description: The framework distinguishes Internalized Mastery (deep domain knowledge built through "sustained cognitive struggle and authentic professional practice across progressive levels of complexity") from Distributed Mastery (proficiency in orchestrating AI systems). The Validation Tether holds that "effective orchestration of opaque AI systems requires independent domain understanding sufficient to recognize when systems operate outside competence boundaries." It separates surface validation (detecting obvious errors and plausibility, attainable without internalized expertise) from substantive validation (detecting domain-specific errors beneath plausible surfaces), which requires Internalized Mastery and an epistemic stance that prompts interrogation of AI outputs. Because commons depletion removes the pathways that build Internalized Mastery, it threatens both expertise forms simultaneously.
requirements: Substantive validation requires internalized domain knowledge that cannot be acquired through observation or AI-assisted performance alone
constraints: Validation Tether refers to a structural relationship between expertise forms, not a trainable disposition; assumes AI outputs remain superficially plausible rather than fully autonomous and reliable
target_learners: Professionals overseeing AI systems in consequential domains
target_learning_goals: Substantive validation of AI outputs
Recognizing when AI operates outside its competence boundaries
examples: The paper illustrates the tether with financial analysts assessing flawed assumptions in risk assessments, physicians checking AI diagnostic recommendations against patient-specific factors, and software engineers detecting maintenance problems in executing code.
key_sources: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602

article_title: Critsly and StudioCrit: An Artefact-Aware AI Critique Workspace and Simulation-Based Readiness Study
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). Critsly and StudioCrit: An Artefact-Aware AI Critique Workspace and Simulation-Based Readiness Study for Design Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00085
title: Validate automated critique classifications with a coding manual, independent coders and reported agreement before deployment claims
description: Before treating machine-assigned cognitive or architectural labels as evidence, the article recommends a human-coder validation study. "A future study should specify a coding manual, define the unit of analysis and have independent coders label an appropriate sample before reconciliation." Agreement should be reported before disagreements are resolved, with Cohen's kappa offered as one established option for nominal labels, and machine-human agreement distinguished from human-human agreement.
requirements: A coding manual and defined unit of analysis
Independent coders labelling an appropriate sample before reconciliation
Agreement statistics reported before disagreements are resolved
constraints: Confidence scores should not be presented as probabilities without calibration evidence
None of the proposed validation activities is a completed result of this report
target_learners: researchers and educators evaluating AI-generated critique classifications
target_learning_goals: establishing validity of automated cognitive and architectural labels of critique activity
examples: The article proposes explicit analysis of ambiguous and low-confidence cases, noting matched verbs are inspectable cues whose presence need not establish a note's cognitive level

article_title: 'Co-pilot won't teach you to be a nurse': nursing academics' perspectives on GenAI use in undergraduate education
citation: Dabkowski, Elissa; Missen, Karen; Allen, Louise; Whitehead, Dean; Worn, Ryan. (2026). 'Co-pilot won't teach you to be a nurse': nursing academics' perspectives on GenAI use in undergraduate education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00220-2
title: Align GenAI integration in nursing education with professional standards and codes of ethics to protect core nursing values
description: Participants held that ethical GenAI use is not a purely technical issue but must stay connected to the NMBA Registered Nurse Standards for Practice, the NMBA Code of Conduct and the ICN Code of Ethics, which emphasise "integrity, accountability, critical thinking, and a commitment to lifelong learning". Some proposed formalised expectations, such as academic standards of practice that students sign up to acknowledging their entry into the profession. The article's recommendations call for nursing-specific guidance aligned with these ethical codes and professional standards.
requirements: Nursing-specific guidance on GenAI clearly aligned with the ethical codes, professional standards and practice expectations of the discipline.
constraints: The article notes the findings reflect a particular point in time as GenAI technologies and institutional responses change quickly.
target_learning_goals: professional identity and ethical conduct
accountability
patient safety
examples: Participants described nursing academics as "the guardians of the profession", responsible to both the university and the patients nurses serve.

article_title: Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills
citation: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864
title: Vantage: a scalable virtual assessment experience for durable skills via human-AI group tasks
description: Vantage is the assessment environment in which "a human subject interacts with one or more AI-based teammates to carry out a joint task" designed to resemble authentic classroom work. An Executive LLM generates all AI teammate responses to steer the conversation toward maximal assessment information, and a separate LLM Evaluator scores transcripts against multi-dimensional rubrics (scores 1-4 plus NA). Users receive a skills map with quantitative competency breakdowns and drill-down excerpts from the conversation exemplifying each score. Rubrics for collaboration, creativity and critical thinking were derived from literature review and refined via expert use on sample conversations.
requirements: A multidimensional scoring rubric for the target skill, derived from the literature and refined where expert agreement was low or raters found it ambiguous
constraints: Coding conversations for conflict resolution and project management proved challenging even after several rounds of rater calibration, with moderate inter-expert agreement
target_learning_goals: Collaboration (conflict resolution, project management)
Creativity
Critical thinking
examples: 188 participants each generated two 30-minute conversations with three AI teammates; tasks included science and debate topics
An Executive LLM focusing on conflict resolution had an AI teammate start a conflict and maintain it until evidence of conflict resolution skill was observed
key_sources: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864

article_title: AI-based digital cheating at university, and the case for new ethical pedagogies
citation: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y
title: Design validity-driven, rehumanised assessments rather than relying on detection and surveillance
description: The article argues that safeguarding academic integrity requires moving beyond detection towards "validity-driven assessment designs that cultivate ethical agency". Its core validity argument is that "an assessment that can be answered by AI in a way that deceives an assessor is an assessment whose answer is intellectually trivial", so the technology exposes assessments that were already failing their fundamental purpose. Rehumanised approaches such as interactive viva-style examinations or peer-mediated assessments are proposed to foster engagement and reduce reliance on AI tools.
requirements: Assessments must genuinely reflect students' understanding and abilities rather than keyword identification, information compilation and paraphrasing
Investment in bespoke, single-use materials tailored to specific learning outcomes
constraints: Bespoke single-use materials take time, which conflicts with contemporary university workload models
Equitable access to resources (digital divides, accommodation quality, caring responsibilities) remains a fundamental barrier to academic integrity
target_learning_goals: deep learning
authentic demonstration of knowledge and ability
ethical formation
examples: Baird and Clare's case used weekly in-class invigilated tests, a red-flag system, random team reassignment, takedown notices, and single-use video case studies to rehumanise and personalise assessment

article_title: Learning after COVID-19 and the ICT career aspirations: Are students entering the AI era with weaker skills?
citation: Popa, D. M., Oprea, S.-V., & Bâra, A. (2022). Learning after COVID-19 and the ICT career aspirations: Are students entering the AI era with weaker skills? Department of Economic Informatics and Cybernetics, Bucharest University of Economic Studies. simona.oprea@csie.ase.ro
title: Latent structural readiness space for digital and AI transformation derived from a variational autoencoder over learning environment indicators
description: The framework trains a variational autoencoder on standardized country-level indicators of autonomy, digital skills and teacher support, projecting them into a two-dimensional latent space interpreted as "a structural readiness space for digital and AI-related transformations in education". Geometric proximity reflects similarity in joint learning environment configurations, and a composite AI Readiness Index is formed as a linear aggregation of the two latent coordinates (α = 0.5). Countries with higher latent readiness tend to show stronger ICT aspiration growth, though the gradient is imperfect.
requirements: Standardized country-level indicators of autonomy, digital skills and teacher support from harmonized PISA data as VAE input
constraints: The article states educational readiness alone does not fully determine ICT aspiration growth, with heterogeneous outcomes among structurally similar countries
target_learners: secondary students across national education systems (PISA populations)
target_learning_goals: digital and AI-era educational readiness; ICT career orientation
examples: The latent space colored by ICT aspiration change (Figure 9) shows a clear but imperfect gradient, and the AI Readiness Index ranking places Korea, Finland, the Netherlands and New Zealand in leading positions

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Respond to GenAI assessment threats with validity-focused redesign that prioritises pedagogy rather than surveillance or prohibition
description: The article's guiding design recommendation is that assessment responses to generative AI should be organised around assessment validity and pedagogy. The authors "contend that assessment twins represent a validity-focused response to GenAI that prioritises pedagogy while supporting meaningful student learning outcomes". Redesign should therefore preserve pedagogically valuable formats and strengthen evidence, rather than simply abandoning vulnerable task types.
requirements: Redesign must keep the targeted learning outcomes and meaningful student learning outcomes central when adapting vulnerable formats.
constraints: The authors acknowledge resource intensity and equity concerns as challenges for this approach.
target_learning_goals: maintaining assessment validity and meaningful learning outcomes in the age of generative AI
examples: The article frames assessment twins as its instantiation of this principle, pairing vulnerable formats so their pedagogical value is retained while evidence is cross-verified.

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Principle of validation authority: delegation is safe exactly where the delegator can validate outputs
description: The article introduces the principle of validation authority, grounded in a bespoke-versus-socially-validated distinction: a library routine is opaque but socially validated through published algorithms, testing, and millions of users, while an AI-generated simulation is opaque and bespoke, "an artifact with a population of one, produced by a stochastic process whose competence boundary is jagged and invisible." The author's generalization is that "delegation is safe exactly where the delegator retains the ability to validate the outputs," which redefines a computational physics course as training validation authority over physical simulations.
requirements: Courses adopting this framing must train disciplinary verification checks the user knows to demand, since a physics simulation's correctness is not observable in use.
constraints: The principle marks a boundary: anyone can delegate in domains like personal productivity apps where correctness is observable in use, but not where correctness must be established by disciplinary checks.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students directing AI agents
target_learning_goals: judgment about when delegation to computational tools is safe and how to validate outputs
examples: The article applies the principle to distinguish a trusted library FFT from a bespoke agent-generated trajectory, noting a wrong trajectory renders as beautifully as a right one.
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation
citation: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://openrouter.ai
title: VARIA four-property formalisation of the AIAA integrity-via-variation hypothesis
description: VARIA formalises the claim that an LLM can generate assessment variant sets that are simultaneously surface-distinct, construct-equivalent, rubric-applicable and difficulty-matched. It "defines a blueprint as a triple of competency, analytic rubric, and canonical solution" and operationalises four properties P1-P4 with metrics (TF-IDF cosine and 4-gram overlap for diversity, an LLM judge for construct equivalence, Flesch reading-ease dispersion for difficulty parity) combined into a joint integrity score J. The framework makes the AIAA claim falsifiable: a generator fails if no prompting setting satisfies all four constraints jointly.
requirements: A blueprint specifying competency, analytic rubric and canonical solution; application-specific thresholds for the four properties; an LLM judge for the construct-equivalence score.
constraints: The pilot's joint score contains no rubric-stability (P3) term and gives surface diversity two of four components; both diversity metrics are lexical, so deep paraphrases of the same scenario could evade them.
target_learners: higher-education students in applied AI and data analytics courses
target_learning_goals: integrity-bearing parallel-forms generation of open-response performance assessment tasks
examples: The pilot instantiates the framework on three blueprints: an audit-style performance task, a data-pipeline bias investigation, and a stakeholder communication task for a model failure.
key_sources: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/u6xef_v2

article_title: VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation
citation: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://openrouter.ai
title: Released VARIA benchmark package with follow-up harness
description: The authors release the VARIA benchmark as a code package containing the three pilot blueprints with rubrics and canonical solutions (blueprints.json), a held-out distant-discipline fourth blueprint (Constructing a Historical Argument from Primary Sources) pre-registered as a generalisation probe, four prompting strategies, five complementary metrics, and an evaluation harness. They "release VARIA together with a ready-to-run follow-up harness" implementing per-variant cross-family judging, the full rubric-stability protocol, and multi-run and larger-N regimes (run_followup.py), plus gap_analysis.py for the paired permutation tests.
requirements: API access to frontier generators and judges; local compute for the GPT-2 reference and metric computation; execution of the pre-registered follow-up protocols.
constraints: The pilot covers only the N = 10 regime of the pre-registered N in {10, 35, 100}; the held-out blueprint B4 is not part of the pilot's 60 cells.
target_learners: higher-education institutions deploying AI-generated assessment variants
target_learning_goals: benchmarking LLM capability to generate construct-equivalent, surface-distinct assessment variants
examples: The pilot executed 57 API-driven generation conditions in approximately 50 minutes plus 3 local GPT-2 conditions in roughly two minutes, at a total cost of approximately ten US dollars.
key_sources: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/u6xef_v2

article_title: Professional communities and student achievement – a meta-analysis
citation: Lomos, C., Hofman, R. H., & Bosker, R. J. (2011). Professional communities and student achievement - a meta-analysis. School Effectiveness and School Improvement, 22(2), 121-148. https://doi.org/10.1080/09243453.2010.550467

description: Because professional community lacks a universal definition and is operationalized inconsistently across studies, the article argues that the concept's key dimensions need conceptual and empirical validation. The article states that "the need for the conceptual and empirical validation of the concept's key dimension was discussed". This principle directs researchers and school designers to establish definitional and measurement validity before drawing on the construct.

constraints: Current operationalization differs across empirical studies, limiting comparability of findings

article_title: Effects of captioning on video comprehension and incidental vocabulary learning
citation: Montero Perez, M., Peters, E., Clarebout, G., & Desmet, P. (2014). Effects of Captioning on Video Comprehension and Incidental Vocabulary Learning. Language Learning & Technology 18(1), 118–141. http://llt.msu.edu/issues/february2014/monteroperezetal.pdf
title: Vanderplank's speculative model of language learning through captioned video: 'taking out' language via attention and adaptation
description: Vanderplank's (1990) model explains how learners extract language from captioned video. The article summarizes it: "the 'taking out' of language from captioned video consists of both attention and adaptation." Attention is a conscious selection process based on "noting and gathering" information plus a reflective component in which learners notice a gap between their L2 knowledge and the captioned input; adaptation is the selection of linguistic elements learners attend to "for [their] own purposes." The study invokes this model to interpret why captioning supported form recognition and clip association.
requirements: Learners must attend to and process the captioned input while watching video for meaning
constraints: The article presents the model as speculative and invokes it as an interpretive frame, not as a tested prediction of this study
target_learning_goals: Incidental vocabulary learning from captioned L2 video
examples: The authors state their form recognition and clip association results "are consistent with Vanderplank's model (1990), in which the role of subtitles was considered crucial to taking out words from captioned input."
key_sources: Montero Perez, M., Peters, E., Clarebout, G., & Desmet, P. (2014). Effects of Captioning on Video Comprehension and Incidental Vocabulary Learning. Language Learning & Technology 18(1), 118–141. http://llt.msu.edu/issues/february2014/monteroperezetal.pdf

article_title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
citation: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031
title: Students using generative AI should ground self-evaluations in valid metacognitive cues rather than perceived ease of AI-assisted problem-solving
description: The article recommends that "To regulate effectively, students using AI tools should focus on valid metacognitive cues instead of the perceived ease of ChatGPT-assisted problem-solving." This follows from its findings that ChatGPT lowered perceived difficulty and effort, yet lower perceived difficulty and higher perceived usefulness of ChatGPT were each associated with overestimating one's performance. Instruction that makes these invalid cues explicit may help learners calibrate self-evaluations of AI-assisted outcomes.
requirements: Learners need awareness that perceived ease and perceived usefulness of AI are unreliable indicators of solution quality and originality
constraints: Supporting evidence is exploratory correlation; the article states these results require further investigation and come from a single laboratory task with limited ecological validity
target_learners: students using generative AI in higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate self-evaluation and metacognitive calibration of AI-assisted problem-solving
examples: The experiment measured self-evaluation bias indices and found higher perceived usefulness of ChatGPT associated with greater overestimation despite no correlation with actual performance

article_title: A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players
citation: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4
title: A profiling game's psychological model must be scientifically validated and must match the profiling intention
description: The article's framework requires that "The psychological model must have been scientifically validated" and that "The chosen psychological model must match the profiling intention", drawing the latter lesson from Silent Hill Shattered Memories, where the psychological model had no strong connection with the intended result. Data must be collected during gameplay and game results must be comparable to those from reliable means such as traditional questionnaires.
requirements: A scientifically validated psychological model with a referential test
Data collected during the gameplay session
Comparability of game results with reliable traditional measures
constraints: Entertainment games using psychological models may not provide results or may lack a strong model-intention connection, as the article reports for Silent Hill
target_learners: players of serious games for assessment and guidance
target_learning_goals: psychological or vocational profiling from gameplay data
examples: The authors selected Holland's RIASEC model for JEU SERAI because it had been scientifically tested since the 1960s and used in vocational guidance tests for decades

citation: Jamaal S. Matthews, Meeta Banerjee, Fani Lauermann. (2014). Academic Identity Formation and Motivation Among Ethnic Minority Adolescents: The Role of the “Self” Between Internal and External Perceptions of Identity. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12318
title: Two-dimensional academic identity framework: internal value and external belonging as distinct but cohabitating dimensions
description: The article frames academic identity as having two concurrently assessed dimensions: an internally negotiated value dimension (perceived importance, interest, and enjoyment of academic tasks) and an externally supported belonging dimension (school belonging and social interconnectedness). It argues that "a multidimensional conceptualization of identity that includes not only internal attributes (i.e., value) but also ecological interactions such as social belonging more adequately captures identity-based processes," and presents value and belonging as "distinct but cohabitating dimensions of academic identity" whose effects on mastery are partially mediated through SRL.

citation: Jan van Aalst. (2009). Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9069-5
title: Discourse coding scheme with seven main codes and 33 subcodes
description: A coding scheme developed to analyze asynchronous group discourse in Knowledge Forum and to identify mechanisms explaining between-group differences in summary-note performance. As printed, "It includes seven main codes: Community, Ideas, Questions, Information, Links, Agency, and Meta-Discourse." Each of 33 subcodes was rated low, medium, or high for its relevance to knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation. citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2023). The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09385-1
title: Design PBL so that learners initiate interactions, since initiating sequences show the strongest association with performance
description: The article argues that which interactions start matters more than how many occur: "Starting or initiating interactions... showed the highest association with performance, pointing to the importance of initiative and sequencing." In the PBL design, the group's sequence of interaction types predicted grades better than raw counts, with information-triggered and argumentation-triggered patterns showing the strongest positive coefficients. Designers should therefore structure online PBL so students - not bulk facilitation - open discussions and episodes.

constraints: Evidence is correlational from one medical PBL course; the facilitated-discussions pattern itself was not significantly associated with grades

examples: In the study, the first-year medical students' weekly problem discussions began online in Moodle forums after a short face-to-face goal-setting session, and information-triggered sessions (beta = 1.72, p = 0.002) showed the largest positive association with grades

article_title: Dynamics of university students’ epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course
citation: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2
title: Valence-activation classification of epistemic emotions
description: The article organises epistemic emotions — "curiosity, enjoyment, surprise, confusion, anxiety, frustration and boredom" — using a valence-activation classification (Pekrun et al., 2017). Enjoyment and curiosity are positive activating emotions; boredom is negative de-activating; surprise is neutral activating, experienced as pleasant or unpleasant; anxiety, confusion and frustration are negative activating emotions that can either drive incongruity-resolution strategies or provoke avoidance. Epistemic emotions arise from cognitive conflict between the known and unknown and are a subset of academic emotions.
requirements: Distinguishes epistemic emotions (tied to knowledge construction) from other academic emotions tied to achievement or social dynamics
constraints: Anxiety, frustration, boredom and enjoyment can also function as achievement or social emotions depending on their focus of attention
target_learners: University students in complex, knowledge-construction learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Supporting knowledge construction and cognitive processing through productive emotional experiences
examples: The study applies the framework to interpret which emotions game sessions activated and how their trajectories related to learning outcomes.

article_title: Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students’ Understanding of Economic Concepts
citation: Ming-fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2005). Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students' Understanding of Economic Concepts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-2811-0
title: Variation theory: for any specific object of learning there is a necessary pattern of variation and invariance learners must experience
description: The article uses a novel learning theory, grounded in phenomenography, as a resource for planning and carrying out teaching. Its central theoretical claim is that "for any specific object of learning there is a necessary pattern of variation and invariance that the learners must experience in order to appropriate the object of learning in question." By bringing out that pattern in the learning situation, the likelihood of the object of learning being appropriated is enhanced. The theory thus links what varies and what stays invariant in a lesson to what learners can discern and appropriate.
requirements: Teaching must be planned so that the necessary pattern of variation and invariance for the specific object of learning is brought out in the learning situation.
constraints: The pattern is specific to the object of learning in question; the article presents the claim as theoretical, supported by one design experiment.
target_learning_goals: understanding of difficult economic concepts, such as how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect market price
examples: Experienced secondary teachers used the theory to plan and carry out three lessons on how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect a good's market price.

citation: Ming Fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2013). Interaction between the learners’ initial grasp of the object of learning and the learning resource afforded. Instructional Science, 41, 1065–1082. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9272-7
title: Variation Theory of Learning: the fundamental conjecture about difference and sameness
description: The Variation Theory of Learning holds that what learners discern and how they learn depends on patterns of variation and invariance in what they experience. Its fundamental conjecture, as printed in the article, is that "new meanings are acquired from experiencing differences against a background of sameness, rather than experiencing sameness against a background of differences." The article tests this conjecture empirically by building the defining patterns of variation and invariance into pedagogical tools for learning an economic principle.
requirements: Patterns of variation and invariance defining the compared conditions must be deliberately built into pedagogical tools such as text, graphs, and worksheets
target_learners: learners studying economics (the price–demand–supply principle) in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: understanding the economic principle of changes in price as a function of changes in the relative magnitude of changes in demand and supply
examples: Two studies embedded variation-consistent versus variation-inconsistent conditions in text, graphs, and worksheets about price changes

article_title: Interaction between the learners’ initial grasp of the object of learning and the learning resource afforded
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2013). Interaction between the learners’ initial grasp of the object of learning and the learning resource afforded. Instructional Science, 41, 1065–1082. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9272-7
title: Embedding patterns of variation and invariance in pedagogical tools (text, graphs, worksheets)
description: A lesson-level design pattern in which the critical aspects of the object of learning are opened up by building patterns of variation and invariance into instructional materials. As the article states, "The patterns of variation and invariance, defining the conditions compared were built into pedagogical tools (text, graphs, and worksheets)." The pattern was applied to the learning of an economic principle in two studies.
requirements: The designer must identify the critical aspects of the object of learning and construct materials that vary some aspects while holding others invariant
constraints: Study 2 shows the choice of tool set must match learners' initial grasp; each set was ineffective for the wrong group
target_learners: learners encountering a new conceptual object of learning, here in economics
target_learning_goals: discerning the relative magnitudes of changes in demand and supply as determinants of price changes
examples: Texts, graphs, and worksheets constructed so that conditions consistent or inconsistent with the variation-theory conjecture were compared

article_title: What matters for students’ learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment!
citation: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x
title: Variation theory as a framework for what students can discern in laboratory learning
description: Variation theory, developed by Marton and colleagues, provides an explanatory framework for the conditions required for learning: it "holds that for learning to be brought about, the critical aspects of the object of learning must be discerned and enter the learner's focal awareness". Central concepts are discernment, simultaneity and variation: people discern aspects by experiencing variation, and the pattern of variation inherent in the learning situation fundamentally influences learning within it. The article uses it to distinguish the intended, enacted and lived objects of learning and to analyse which critical features each lab technology makes discernible.
requirements: A pattern of variation in the learning situation that makes the critical aspect of the object of learning vary while other aspects remain invariant
constraints: Results and conclusions are also consistent with conceptual conflict and cognitive conflict theories, so the framework is not uniquely required
target_learners: science and engineering students in laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: discerning critical features of physical concepts such as velocity, change of velocity and acceleration
examples: The article analyses whether motion up, down and at the turning point can be studied in each lab, since studying only downward motion gives position, velocity and acceleration the same sign, restricting discrimination between the concepts

article_title: Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study
citation: Kristoffer Larsson · Klas Andersson. (2025). Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1025–1046. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09721-y
title: Variation theory of learning and teaching: learning as discerning new aspects of a phenomenon through systematic patterns of variation (contrast, then generalization)
description: Variation theory is a general learning theory with an aligned teaching theory, in which learning means becoming able to handle a phenomenon in a more powerful way in novel situations by discerning a new aspect of it. The article states that "The pattern to be presented first is called contrast and is considered to be the vehicle of learning", opening up the aspect by juxtaposing values against an invariant case. Contrast is followed by the generalization pattern, where "each value, one at a time, of the aspect is kept invariant while varying the cases", so students see the aspect applies across cases. The study applied this to the aspect of alternating points of view on societal issues.
requirements: Systematic introduction of the patterns of variation in the specified order, with the case kept invariant during contrast and the value kept invariant during generalization
constraints: The theory's application to critical thinking had been theoretically developed but not extensively empirically tested before this study
target_learning_goals: Alternating between points of view when reasoning about societal issues
examples: Teachers showed four student responses to a voting-age task differing from zero to three alternations of points of view, then generalized across voting-age, referendum and wage-difference tasks value by value.

article_title: Teachers’ learning in a learning study
citation: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1
title: Variation theory: learning as discernment, simultaneity and variation of critical aspects
description: Variation theory analyzes learning on the basis of "the concepts discernment, simultaneity and variation", all three of which the article says are required for learning to be possible. Learning is defined as a new way to experience the environment, in which the learner discerns new aspects of a phenomenon simultaneously with other aspects and combines them into a whole. In the study, teachers used this framework to identify the critical aspects of English learning objects and to organize contrasts in instruction, e.g. contrasting singular and plural forms of to be.
requirements: A variation must be offered, i.e. a number of different aspects that can be experienced, so the learner can discern new aspects of the phenomenon
constraints: Knowledge of an aspect cannot be developed if only one example has been experienced, as in the article's apple example where variation of apples is needed to discern taste
target_learners: pupils aged 9-11 in school years 4-5 learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: discerning critical aspects of English grammar learning objects such as possessive pronouns and the verbs to be and to have
examples: Teachers planned lessons by first answering what it takes to develop knowledge about the object of learning, identifying critical aspects such as discerning that the pronoun you can be both singular and plural

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: Variation theory of learning: learning is discernment of critical aspects through experienced variation
description: Variation theory holds that "learning primarily involves a qualitative change in the way we experience something in the world around us", and that experiencing a phenomenon in a particular way requires that certain "critical aspects" be discerned simultaneously. Its core mechanism is that "the necessary condition for discernment is 'experienced variation' on the part of the learner": to discern an aspect such as colour, a learner must experience at least two different values of it while other aspects are kept invariant. In learning study, teachers use the theory to design patterns of variation and invariance that enable students to discern the critical aspects of the object of learning.
requirements: Teachers must identify the critical aspects of the object of learning that students must discern
The lesson must enact a pattern in which the targeted aspect varies while other aspects are kept invariant
constraints: The article notes a gap can exist between theory and practice, revealed only by carefully studying what happened in the lesson
target_learning_goals: discerning critical aspects of curricular objects of learning such as fractions and reaction rates
examples: In the mathematics case, the teacher varied the denominator while keeping the numerator invariant, then contrasted equal and unequal splits of a pizza

article_title: Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings
citation: Moreno, L., Briñol, P., & Petty, R. E. (2022). Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 139–165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09270-y
title: Build learner confidence only after ensuring the underlying thoughts are positive; confidence in negative self-thoughts backfires
description: This principle holds that interventions raising learners' metacognitive confidence will amplify whatever performance-relevant thoughts the learner already holds. The article shows that "when thoughts were positive, increased confidence in the primary cognitions improved performance," but the same confidence validating negative thoughts reduced performance. Educators should therefore establish positive performance-relevant cognitions (about the self, the task, or the exam) before or alongside any confidence-boosting induction, and should not assume confidence is uniformly beneficial.
requirements: The learner's dominant performance-relevant thoughts must be diagnosed before applying a confidence induction
Confidence inductions (e.g., recalling past episodes of confidence) must follow the thought-valence induction to validate the intended cognitions
constraints: Confidence in negative thoughts reduces performance, so confidence boosters can backfire
Validation processes are more likely to operate when learners are motivated to think and the topic is personally relevant
target_learners: students facing exams or performance assessments
target_learning_goals: improving performance on knowledge tests and standardized assessments
fostering positive self-relevant beliefs about academic ability
examples: In Study 3, participants who listed positive thoughts about their qualities as students and then recalled a past confidence episode scored higher on GRE questions than those who recalled doubt
In Study 2, validating negative self-thoughts led participants to solve fewer geometric-shape problems than invalidating those same thoughts

description: The article frames valued thinking in education as a historical narrative whose contemporary manifestations are higher-order thinking (HOT), critical thinking (CT), and critical-analytic thinking (CAT). The authors state their purpose is "to forward a narrative of valued thinking in education—manifested as higher-order (HOT), critical thinking (CT), and critical-analytic thinking (CAT)—by overviewing its past and present, possible future." article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Research results are valid only when the learner is consonant with and can appropriate the mediational means of the research as useful cultural tools
description: The article proposes that "Research results, I propose, are only valid when the learner is consonant with and can appropriate the mediational means of the research as useful cultural tools." Under this conception, valid research is inherently instructional, because the congruence of learner and learning materials affords development; conversely, valid teaching represents inquiry. The principle treats researcher and teacher as parallel mediators, each needing the learner's shared sense of telos and intersubjective agreement on task and tool use.
requirements: The learner must share the researcher's or teacher's sense of telos, and the mediational means must build on the learner's prior culturally fostered tool use; instruction fails when there is little or no congruence and no reciprocal relationship regarding appropriate tool use.
constraints: The article states this conception of validity holds only under the particular conception of Vygotsky's ZPD outlined in the essay, which is itself one selective reading among competing appropriations.
target_learning_goals: development through the zone of proximal development
appropriation of cultural tools for thinking
examples: The article cites Moll and Greenberg's (1990) finding that instruction failed when formal schooling was incongruent with students' prior culturally fostered tool use, and Heath's (1991) point that school mediational means must be congruent with students' prior learning experiences.

citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net

citation: Ertugruloglu, E.O.; Mearns, T.L.; Admiraal, W.F. (2023). Scaffolding what, why and how? A critical thematic review study of descriptions, goals, and means of language scaffolding in Bilingual education contexts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100550

description: The review adopts Van de Pol et al.'s (2010) framework, which distinguishes scaffolding goals from scaffolding means and specifies characteristics of scaffolding, as its analytic lens. It uses this framework "to synthesize the various forms that scaffolding of language takes in the teaching practice of subject teachers teaching in bilingual secondary education contexts". article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Vector autoregression (VAR) as an analytical method for temporal relationships between emotions and language behaviours
description: The review introduces vector autoregression as a statistical technique for analysing how a vector of observations at a given time-point is influenced by vectors of observations at previous time-points. In the simplest VAR(1) model, observations at time t are regressed on observations at time t-1; higher-order models capture dependencies at further distances. Its power lies in accounting for both within-variable and between-variable dynamics, revealing how a variable's future values are predicted by its own past values and by past values of other variables, addressing temporal relationships that the review says have never been validly explored in SLA emotion studies.
requirements: Intensive longitudinal time series data on the emotions and language behaviours of interest, collected at a sampling rate matching the timescale of the hypothesized temporal relationships
target_learners: Second language learners studied at individual or group level
target_learning_goals: Identifying temporal (auto-)correlations among emotions and language behaviours to inform timely interventions
examples: The review illustrates that if a hypothetical VAR model showed anxiety at a previous time-point positively predicting later anxiety while negatively predicting enjoyment, educators could design interventions that proactively address anxiety before it undermines enjoyment

article_title: Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write
citation: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X
title: Parallel processing of spelling and graphomotor modules in handwriting production (van Galen's model)
description: The article frames handwriting production within van Galen's (1991) psychomotor model, in which spelling (high-level) and graphomotor (low-level) modules operate in parallel, with higher modules running ahead of real-time output. The study's findings are taken to support this account: the authors write that their finding "supports the idea of a parallel activation of spelling (high-level) and graphomotor (low-level) modules". The related parallel and cascading model (Olive, 2014) makes the dynamics of this parallel processing flexible according to the cognitive resources allocated to spelling versus motor control.

constraints: The article notes further studies are necessary to better understand the emergence of the cascading phenomenon between spelling and motor processes in learning to write

target_learning_goals: learning to spell words and to form cursive letters fluently
examples: Grade 1 students produced more stops when writing a difficult first letter in a low-frequency word, which the authors read as spelling processes interfering with motor processing

article_title: Validation processes and reading purpose: Is validation against knowledge and prior text influenced by reading goal?
citation: Moort, M. L. van, Koornneef, A. W., Wilderjans, T. F., & Broek, P. W. van den. (2022). Validation processes and reading purpose: Is validation against knowledge and prior text influenced by reading goal? Journal of Educational Psychology, 114(7), 1533-1552. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000769
title: Two-component architecture of validation: coherence-detection and postdetection epistemic elaboration
description: The article describes theoretical models of validation that assume distinct components: a coherence-detection component involved in detecting (in)consistencies, and a postdetection processing component involving optional epistemic elaboration to resolve inconsistencies. The coherence-detection component is described as "a routine part of comprehension" that is "memory-based, pose little demands on cognitive resources, and are not dependent on readers' goals." Postdetection elaboration processes are "slow, resource-demanding and under strategic control of the reader." Two named models instantiate this architecture: the RI-Val model (resonance, integration, validation) and the two-step model of validation (epistemic monitoring followed by epistemic elaboration).

constraints: The coherence-detection component is assumed to be passive and not under strategic control of the reader
Epistemic elaboration only occurs when readers are motivated and have enough cognitive resources available
target_learning_goals: Monitoring text coherence and accuracy during reading
Building accurate mental representations of text content
examples: The study tested predictions from this architecture by examining whether reading goals modulate coherence-detection (they did not) versus postdetection representation-building (they did, for congruent targets)

article_title: Emotional transmission in the classroom: Exploring the relationship between teacher and student enjoyment.
citation: Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Lüdtke, O., Pekrun, R., & Sutton, R. E. (2009). Emotional Transmission in the Classroom: Exploring the Relationship Between Teacher and Student Enjoyment. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(3), 705–716. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0014695
title: Social–cognitive value-induction account of emotional transmission from teachers to students
description: The article frames teacher-to-student enjoyment transmission using social–cognitive learning theories and social construction approaches. Students can learn that a task is valuable by observing their teacher's enjoyment, a process the article calls "value induction" (citing Pekrun, 2000), also described as "appreciation-oriented modeling" (Brophy, 2004). Wild et al.'s constructive social perception model holds that even implicit hints about a target's motivational orientation elicit perceivers' expectations of enjoyment, which then shape students' own enjoyment. The article operationalizes the behavioral side of this account as teacher enthusiasm and tests it via mediation analysis.
requirements: Teachers' enjoyment must be made visible through socially perceivable behavior (enthusiasm) for transmission to occur
constraints: The account was tested in mathematics classrooms with students aged 13–15 in Bavaria; the authors argue basic mechanisms should generalize but call for tests in other domains and age groups
target_learning_goals: students' pleasant achievement emotions, specifically enjoyment of learning
examples: Wild et al.'s experiments: participants taught by seemingly extrinsically motivated teachers reported lower interest and less task enjoyment than those taught by seemingly intrinsically motivated teachers, despite identical lessons

title: Analyze behavioral variability as a functional signal rather than noise, using single-trial modeling
description: Because within-subject trial-to-trial fluctuations dominated behavior across all three tasks, the article recommends treating variability as informative state-dependent dynamics rather than measurement noise. The authors recommend that "Future studies should adopt single-trial modeling (e.g., Hidden Markov or state-space models) to capture latent state transitions and nonlinear interactions", since trial-averaged analyses may obscure rapid state-dependent fluctuations central to predictive control.
requirements: Single-trial data collection with dense trial repetition per condition, since trial-averaged analyses risk masking dynamic processes.
constraints: The recommendation arises from a sensorimotor task setting with 54 participants and may not transfer directly to other learning domains.
target_learning_goals: understanding trial-to-trial behavioral variability in adaptive control
examples: The authors found within-subject variability exceeded between-subject variability by roughly an order of magnitude across all tasks and proposed Hidden Markov or state-space models for future work.

title: Validate and adjust pre-trained LLM embeddings before using them for task-specific formative assessment
description: The article argues that because pre-trained embeddings may not capture the nuances that matter in science education assessment, LLM-based formative assessment systems need "adjustments and validation on the specific task" before deployment. Effectiveness of a Program Based on A Multi-Sensory Strategy in Developing Visual Perception of Primary School Learners with Learning Disabilities: A Contextual Study of Arabic Learners. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 8(1), 72-104. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2019.3346
title: VAKT (visual, auditory, kinesthetic-tactile) multi-sensory strategy based on the Fernald method
description: The article frames its intervention within the VAKT tradition: "This strategy is based on the Vernald method, also known as the visual, auditory, kinesthetic-tactile (VAKT) which refers to learning by using the senses primarily in education and teaching learners with learning difficulties". Hearing, seeing, touching and movement are applied together so learners draw on sensorimotor memories to recognize texts. The article defines the multi-sensory strategy generally as one that "focuses on the use of different senses in teaching processes to resolve educational problems", and cites prior studies reporting its effectiveness for memory, reading and writing difficulties.
requirements: Teaching must simultaneously engage visual, auditory and kinesthetic channels so that learners connect sensorimotor experiences to the text or reading materials
constraints: The article presents the strategy in the context of learners with learning difficulties, particularly primary-school age children who tend to use most of their senses to identify environmental stimuli
target_learning_goals: visual perception
decoding and reading skills
memory of new skills
examples: The study's program had learners identify everyday articles using multiple senses and infer details of shape, size, color, materials and components of displayed visual stimuli

article_title: Painting with the Multiple Intelligences: Defining Student Success and Permanence in Art Class
citation: Şeyda Eraslan Taşpınar, Ali Kaya. (2016). Painting with the Multiple Intelligences: Defining Student Success and Permanence in Art Class. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1684
title: Use varied teaching methods and techniques rather than a single method so all students are reached
description: From the study's findings and suggestions, the authors recommend that in planning and applying classes, "instead of the use of only one teaching method and technique, all students should be reached by using different teaching methods and techniques", because students' interests, learning styles and abilities differ. They also call for developing new MIT-based teaching methods to turn student differences into advantages in visual arts education.
requirements: Teachers plan activities suited to differing student interests, learning styles and abilities
constraints: The authors note their results come from one student group and class and recommend longer studies on larger groups
target_learners: all students in a classroom, including those with differing intelligence profiles
target_learning_goals: increasing student success and knowledge permanence
examples: The experimental group's three-week programme used story writing, symmetry analysis, guided picture questioning, role play, song writing, buzz-group discussion, diary writing and object naming instead of a single method

article_title: The Effectiveness of Visualization, Auditory, Kinesthetic (VAK) Model toward Writing Narrative: Linguistic Intelligence Perspective
citation: Kusumawarti, E., Subiyantoro, S., & Rukayah. (2020). The Effectiveness of Visualization, Auditory, Kinesthetic (VAK) Model toward Writing Narrative: Linguistic Intelligence Perspective. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 677-694. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13442a
title: VAK model: learning structured around visual, auditory, and kinesthetic styles in four steps
description: The VAK model "combines three learning styles namely learning by seeing (visual), learning by listening (auditory) and learning by motion and emotions (kinesthetic)", giving students flexibility to use one, two, or all three styles. In this study it was implemented in language learning through four steps: "preparation, delivery, training, and the display of results". In the delivery step teachers used powerpoints and videos for visual and auditory learners and had students demonstrate experiences for kinesthetic learners; the training step used group discussion and brief narrative drafting; the final step shared and consolidated discussion results.
requirements: Teachers prepare learning devices, condition the class, and motivate students in the preparation step
Media such as powerpoints and learning videos, plus demonstration and discussion activities matched to the three styles
constraints: The article notes some students with auditory styles may find it difficult to decipher a series of phonemes quickly, so linguistic intelligence "will not be maximized" in that part
target_learning_goals: narrative writing skills
language learning
examples: In the study the experimental class was taught with VAK steps of preparation, delivery, training, and appearance of results, with powerpoint media and experience-telling demonstrations

article_title: Improving Students' Van Hiele Level of Geometric Thinking Using Geometer's Sketchpad
citation: Poh Geik Tieng & Leong Kwan Eu. (2013). Improving Students' Van Hiele Level Of Geometric Thinking Using Geometer's Sketchpad. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 2(3). www.mojet.net
title: van Hiele model of geometric thinking levels
description: The van Hiele model describes students' geometric thought as five hierarchical levels: "recognition, analysis, ordering, deduction, and rigor (Van Hiele, 1986)". The study operationalizes the lower levels for angles: Level 0 for students unable to distinguish angle types, Level 1 for recognizing and naming figures visually, and Level 2 for identifying figures by their specific geometric properties. The Malaysian Year 4 syllabus targets only up to Level 2.
requirements: Assessment items distinguishing visualization of angles (Level 1) from concluding properties of angles (Level 2), with criteria such as 2 of 3 and 2 of 2 correct items
constraints: The study applies only Levels 0-2, appropriate for primary pupils; the article cites Battista (2002) that the theory best describes thinking about two-dimensional shapes
target_learning_goals: Progressing from visual recognition of angle types to identifying angle properties
examples: The study's three pre/post tests scored students on right, acute, and obtuse angles at Levels 1 and 2

title: VARK learning styles model (visual, auditory, read, kinesthetic)
description: The VARK model, developed by Fleming, classifies students into four learner types: "Visual, Auditory, Read, and Kinesthetic". Students with one style are unimodal and those with more than one are multimodal. The article states VARK "refer to the aspect of sensory modalities", linking style optimization to memory, and reports the styles are relatively stable and easy to implement across education levels. The study used Fleming's (2001) young-category questionnaire adapted for Indonesian elementary students.
requirements: Learning style measured with the VARK questionnaire (version 7 for young learners), with bimodal and multimodal classifications excluded when percentages are very small
constraints: The article disregarded the visual learning style because the number of visual students was too small to meet data analysis requirements
target_learning_goals: identifying students' preferred sensory modality for managing learning information
examples: Students classified via a 16-item questionnaire with four answer options (V, A, R, K); e.g., a student scoring V = 2, A = 4, R = 2, K = 8 was assigned the K style

title: Novel bench-top vascular anastomosis simulation model with integrated leakage testing system
description: A low-cost bench-top platform for end-to-end and side-to-side vascular anastomosis practice, consisting of "an A5-sized plastic board with two adjustable metal clamps secured 15 cm apart" holding PTFE grafts. An integrated leakage testing system uses a peristaltic pump with intraluminal pressure maintained at or below 120 mmHg to grade anastomotic leakage (Grades 0–3), providing immediate structured feedback after suturing practice.

title: VAP Prevention Performance Checklist: a 23-item, 0–46-point observational skill instrument validated by two-round Delphi
description: The researchers developed the VAP Prevention Performance Checklist to evaluate students' performance of skills that contribute to VAP prevention, based on relevant literature and guidelines. article_title: Augmented reality for teaching undergraduate human anatomy: An educators' perspective.
citation: Williams A, Sun Z, Vaccarezza M. (2026). Augmented reality for teaching undergraduate human anatomy: An educators' perspective. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70214
title: Value-based design as a framework for directing AR development in anatomy education
description: The article proposes value-based design as an approach to direct future technological development in anatomy education, incorporating the nuanced perspectives of expert anatomy educators. It would "direct energy away from finding ‘what works’" and instead "require the involvement of all affected stakeholders to establish sustainable and flexible technological solutions which move beyond novelty or immediate scalability." The article uses this framework to argue that current AR innovations have neglected sustainable institutional infrastructure and that educators value accurate content, seamless interfacing, and curriculum-supporting features.
requirements: Involvement of all affected stakeholders beyond the end user
constraints: Must not be implemented at the expense of proven teaching methods or further burden faculty time and resources
target_learning_goals: Human anatomy education

citation: Tümsek Gizem Solmaz and Akmeşe Zehra Baykal. (2026). Reducing parents’ vaccination hesitancy: a new educational training model in Turkish sample. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1808239
title: Vaccine Opposition Scale (VOS)
description: The Vaccine Opposition Scale (VOS), developed by Kılınçarslan et al., is a "21-item, 5-point Likert-type scale designed to assess attitudes toward vaccination". It comprises four subscales: Benefits, Antagonism, Alternative Solutions, and Justification of Hesitancy, with higher scores indicating greater vaccine hesitancy. In this study, Cronbach's alpha coefficients for the subscales ranged between 0.859 and 0.928, indicating high reliability. The VOS was used as the primary outcome measure before and after the NETM intervention.
requirements: Participants literate in Turkish (scale developed and validated in Turkish)
constraints: Assesses attitudes toward vaccination, not actual vaccination behavior

examples: Used as pre-test and post-test measure in the 50-parent NICU study

article_title: Integrating formative and summative feedback in online situational judgement tests: effects of feedback design on medical students' motivational and cognitive learning factors.
citation: Reiser, S., Schick, K., Pittroff, S. I. D., Janssen, L., Berberat, P. O., Gartmeier, M., & Bauer, J. (2026). Integrating formative and summative feedback in online situational judgement tests: effects of feedback design on medical students’ motivational and cognitive learning factors. Medical Education Online, 31(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2026.2639198
title: VA-MeCo SJT with five integrated automated feedback versions implemented in Moodle
description: The VA-MeCo is a video-based situational judgement test assessing medical communication competence on three dimensions (advancing the conversation's content, providing structure, building relationship with the patient), with 117 items nested in eleven scenarios. For this study the authors developed five feedback versions: "We developed four versions of task-based (formative) feedback, differing in their enrichment strategies (i.e. reflection prompts or expert explanations) and the timing of the feedback (i.e. immediate feedback or post-test feedback)", plus one performance-based Summative Test Profile with sub-test scores and social comparison. Technical implementation used the open-source learning management system Moodle to ensure transferability.
requirements: Automated delivery via the Moodle learning management system
Expert validation of the ~350-word explanations by five subject matter experts in medical communication
A user-centred design and programming approach focused on usability and acceptance by students and faculty
constraints: The evaluation used a shortened 14-item test version with three scenarios rather than the full 117-item test to keep participant workload manageable
No reflection training was given before the reflection-based conditions, to avoid confounding the feedback manipulation
target_learners: medical students across all stages of medical education
target_learning_goals: medical communication competence (content advancement, providing structure, building relationship)
examples: Cognitive interviews with five subject matter experts, four experts and sixteen medical students found all versions clear, easy to comprehend, and cognitively and motivationally engaging

article_title: The impact of an immersive virtual reality anatomy lab for informal science education.
citation: Alkhammash L, Saraco AN, Goes Schaurich C, Lo BSY, Krebs C. (2025). The impact of an immersive virtual reality anatomy lab for informal science education. Anat Sci Educ. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70087
title: VanVR APP: an immersive, gesture-based virtual anatomy lab built from consented, digitized anatomical specimens
description: The Vancouver Virtual Reality Anatomy and Pathology Project (VanVR APP) is a fully immersive, interactive virtual anatomy lab built in Unity on Meta Quest 3 headsets, designed to mimic UBC's gross anatomy lab. It offers "fully annotated high-resolution 3D anatomical specimens" interacted with via "symmetrical virtual hand gesture control instead of hand-held controllers."
